messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 53
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Ship Captain
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
- Pcl5: 71

# Vignette: Fatima

Fatima is a 53-year-old married woman of Lebanese descent who has spent the better part of three decades commanding cargo vessels across the Mediterranean, the Arabian Gulf, and beyond. She carries herself with the kind of quiet authority that comes from years of navigating unpredictable seas and managing crews who initially doubted whether a woman belonged on the bridge. Those who work under her describe her as precise, unflappable, and fair. What they do not see is what happens when the ship is quiet and the night watch has taken over and Fatima is alone in her cabin with nothing between her and her own mind.

She grew up in Beirut, the eldest of five children, in a household governed by her father's moods. He was a man of enormous physical strength and almost no emotional restraint, and from the time Fatima was very young, his anger landed on her body. The beatings were not random — they followed a logic she spent her childhood trying to decode, believing that if she could just be careful enough, quiet enough, invisible enough, she could prevent the next one. She never could. Her mother witnessed much of it and said nothing, a silence Fatima experienced as its own kind of violence. By the time she was sixteen she had learned to dissociate during the worst moments, to go somewhere else inside herself while her body absorbed what it absorbed. She left home at eighteen for maritime school and never lived under her father's roof again.

For many years the sea felt like salvation. The structure of shipboard life — watches, protocols, chain of command — gave her a world she could actually control. She married a kind man, a marine engineer she met during her early career, and they built a life together that felt, on the surface, stable. She rarely spoke about her childhood. She told herself she had left it behind.

The unraveling began gradually, though she can now trace it back to a specific evening three years ago when a crew member — a large, heavyset man — shoved a younger deckhand during a heated argument on the bridge. The shove was brief, almost incidental, but something in Fatima locked. She gave the orders she needed to give, separated the men, filed the report. Then she went to her cabin, sat on the edge of her bunk, and shook for two hours. She did not understand what had happened to her.

Since then, the past has become increasingly present. She wakes at three or four in the morning convinced she can hear her father's footsteps in the corridor outside her cabin, that particular heavy, deliberate tread she memorized as a child. Her heart is already pounding before she is fully conscious. She lies rigid, listening, until the sounds of the ship reassert themselves. During the day she startles violently at raised voices, at the sound of a door slamming, at any sudden movement in her peripheral vision. She has begun avoiding the crew mess when she knows certain men will be there — men who are loud, who gesture broadly, who take up space in the way her father did.

She is irritable with her husband in ways she recognizes as unfair and cannot seem to stop. She tells him she is tired, which is true, but it is not the whole truth. The whole truth is that she no longer feels safe inside her own body, that the woman who has navigated storms and piracy threats and equipment failures in the middle of open water cannot navigate the distance between who she is now and who she was in that apartment in Beirut.

She describes her childhood in careful, measured language, the way she might file a damage report — factual, contained, stripped of emotion. But her hands grip the arms of the chair when she speaks, and her eyes go somewhere far away, and it is clear that the distance she crossed to get here was not only geographical.
